failures.criterion: README 'Take-over' (and the docs criterion 'packages/envoy/cmd/listener docs say what is true'): on a graceful stop per-session order is kept, because the stopping pod NAKs what it has not handled and the durable redelivers it before newer messages.
failures.evidence: Red test packages/envoy/cmd/listener/multiprocess_test.go TestTwoPodsGracefulStopWithMessagesOnTheWireKeepsOrder, shown failing in 3 of 3 runs by `cd packages/envoy && go test -tags multiprocess -count=3 -run '^TestTwoPodsGracefulStopWithMessagesOnTheWireKeepsOrder$' -v ./cmd/listener`: 'ses_mp_wirestop_one took evt-mp-0063 (published 3.1s, prompted 3.578s ...) before evt-mp-0055 (published 2.701s, prompted 8.705s ...), out of the publish order'. The active pod's link has a 300 ms delay, so messages are on the wire when it unsubscribes on SIGTERM. They come back exactly one ack wait (6 s) later, after the standby delivered newer ones. [inference from the 6 s delay: they are dropped without a NAK.] Without the delay, a throwaway row with two pods and a message every 2 ms failed 1 of 3 runs: 'evt-mp-1280 after 6.363s (published -357ms after the SIGTERM)', prompted after evt-mp-1284. A SIGKILL-then-SIGTERM row failed the same way once in 7 runs (evt-mp-0080 prompted 6.003 s after evt-mp-0082). Either the stop must keep order, or the README must stop claiming it.

risks: Graceful stop soon after a node loss: while the lost pod's connection lingers, each next holder settles for about one ack wait (about 6 s), and a second graceful stop during a settle starts the wait again. With SIGTERMs 3 s apart, messages published after the first SIGTERM arrived 9.37-9.48 s after it (3 runs), just under the 10 s graceful bound. [inference] A second stop 4-6 s after the first would exceed 10 s.
